justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—one day, one week, and one month—were driven by a combination of the most recent observed data and baseline trends within the system being forecasted. These estimates assume that, absent any significant external shocks or deviations, the underlying dynamics of the process will remain steady over these timeframes. Because we used the same central point estimate for all three horizons, it suggests that our model assumes stability in the short term, with no strong reason to predict a directional shift in the value. Essentially, the underlying conditions driving the forecast are expected to hold steady, at least on average.

The confidence intervals (CIs) widen as the time horizon increases, reflecting growing uncertainty over time. This occurs because, in probabilistic forecasting, the future becomes less predictable the farther out you look. For a one-day forecast, the primary source of uncertainty might be small short-term fluctuations or noise in the system. For a one-week or one-month timeframe, however, additional variables such as compounding random fluctuations, changes in broader market conditions, or unforeseen events introduce more variability. This is why the one-month interval, spanning from 673.95 to 758.19, is much wider than the one-day interval of 709.91 to 722.23.

As for risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals, these would typically be extreme or unexpected factors that the model cannot account for. For example, sudden and significant external shocks—such as a major regulatory change, geopolitical tensions, or a financial market crash—could invalidate the assumptions behind the forecast. Additionally, structural changes in the underlying system, such as a shift in demand-supply dynamics or an unforeseen technological breakthrough, might make the actual outcomes differ substantially from these predictions. Such rare but impactful events are often not captured well in standard modeling approaches, which focus on the most likely range of outcomes. Therefore, while the model provides a reasonable range of expectations based on known variability, it cannot entirely rule out extreme outliers.
